utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. To enable the protected witness to enter the courtroom, the blinds should be brought down and the witness may then be brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please sit down. Good morning, sir. You wait a moment so that the blinds could be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, good morning, sir. The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth still applies and the protective measures are still in place. Mr. Tolimir, you may continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God be of assistance to all and may there be peace unto this house. And may God's will be done in these proceedings and the outcome as God wishes and not as I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stopped off yesterday when we were showing document 1D129, it is an exhibit, and the witness said that he wasn't aware of the document and that he never talked to these women that Naser Oric referred to. My question is as follows: Was the Srebrenica zone demilitarised or not? In view of your yesterday's statement where you said that a forward command post was set up in the area around the protected zone - thank you - in the area around the enclave.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I knew at the time is what I said, and that's what was the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the zone demilitarised or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the information that we received, it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you aware of the position UNPROFOR took in relation to the demilitarised zone and was it tolerant in its conduct toward the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer the question. I wasn't near there. I was not in touch with either other UNPROFOR or the zone itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, did you know that a group of commanders from Zepa and Srebrenica, headed by Naser Oric, in April of 1995, arrived in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps of the BH army, and that that toured the defence lines in Kladanj, the brigades in Teocak, Sapna, Medjedja, Seonica, and Kakanj? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this at all. What I can tell you is that I heard perhaps in 1996 that some of the commanders had gone out of there earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if you know that the -- whether this group of commanders and senior officers which came out of Srebrenica and Zepa, whether they were received by Alija Izetbegovic in Kakanj. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not aware of this. I was a commander of a unit attached to the staff. I was not an acquaintance of these commanders, I was not in touch with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, if you know, that this group of commanders in April of 1995, that's to say, before Srebrenica and Zepa, were in your area of responsibility with General Delic, with the chief of the Main Staff of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, was this group received by your commander, Sead Delic?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. At that time I went rarely to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that this group of senior officers from Srebrenica and Zepa in the month of April met up with the command of your corps in Tuzla; is this something that you learned from your commander and other senior officers and your -- or your subordinates who happened to be in the command at the time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, you keep asking these questions but I'm not familiar with this group at all. I don't know these people and I've only heard of Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, this group of commanders were they part of preparations for the joining up of the enclaves with the commander of the Main Staff, the commanders of -- the commander of the corps, and commanders of the brigades that they toured in Sapna and Medjedja?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only keep repeating what I've already said. I really have no idea, to be frank, as to when these people came, where, who they met with, and I don't know any of them. I've never met with them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, what was your level in the corps command at the time and were you involved in these preparations and meetings; and if you were not, why not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I was a commander of a unit attached to the staff. I would send reports to the commander on the situation in the unit every week or every fortnight, and as for all the other goings-on, the commander had his assistants charged with various specialities and he would be better placed to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 1D31, page 1, lines 19, 20, 21, and 22. Or rather, my apologies, before this appears on the screen -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up D1, page 5, lines 22 and 23, and then lines 32 and lines 46, and that will make things easier for the witness. It will make my question more understandable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you sure you're asking for document D1? Is that on the screen now? Thank you. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we turn to page 5, please. Yes. The witness should be able to see it. It's the fourth paragraph, line 2. I'll read the two lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "In late April 1995 we took off by helicopter from Zepa and arrived in Zenica. It was a delegation that was dispatched from Srebrenica headed by Commander Naser Oric." And rather than read the whole statement, let's go to item 32 and see -- or rather, line 32 - can you mark that for the witness? - to see what happened when they arrived in Zenica. And it is stated here: "From Zenica, all the members of the delegation were transferred to Kakanj. And the invalids who had come along with us were transferred to the other side. We were received by the Chief of Staff, General Hadzihasanovic in Kakanj and discussions took place around the events in Srebrenica. That was the reason why we got there. We were supposed to go on from there to Tuzla. In the meantime, the commander of the General Staff, Delic, arrived, who arranged a helicopter for us to transfer us to Visca, from where we were transported to the corps command where Delic said the commander received us. Subsequently we had meetings with Governor Izet Hadzic. On the following day we toured the defence lines in Kladanj, above the tunnel, and the following day we visited the command of the Teocak brigade, Sapna, Medjedja, Snjeznica. And the following day we went to Kakanj. President Izetbegovic got there and we talked to him." That's where I'll end my quotation. This is a statement by an eye-witness who was present at the meeting. Do you still deny that these activities had indeed taken place in the area of responsibility of your corps in Tuzla prior to the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I don't think that we have the right document on the screen or even not the right page of the document. We can't find this portion you were quoting. Can you help us? Of course I'm referring to the English page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will now do my best -- or rather, my legal advisor will try and indicate for you the references in the English version. Since I don't speak English, I'm merely reading from page 5 of the statement, which we received from the Prosecution. Thank you. Mr. President, it's page 6 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And which paragraph and line?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 3, up until the line starting with Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, it could be helpful if you would repeat the question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us if you knew anything of these activities and whether this eye-witness speaks truthfully about the activities which happened in the area of responsibility of your corps and have -- and had to do with Srebrenica and Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that I have never seen this report before. Secondly, I don't know the person who gave the statement. My answer can only be: I don't know, perhaps yes, perhaps not. I was not involved in these activities and I had no information at the time. Fourthly, I can say that of the entire list of people mentioned here, I know only two persons. I knew them from before the war, and yet I had contact with these people during the war only rarely, very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Based on the activities described by this eye-witness, can you conclude that this was a delegation of commanders from Srebrenica and Zepa who came to the corps command to attend preparations for an operation aimed at joining up the enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa with the area of responsibility of the corps, and this took place in April of 1995 before the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say really is maybe yes and maybe not, but I had nothing to do with these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D31 on our screens now, page 1, lines 19, 20, 21, and 22. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2. In English that will be page 2 and in B/C/S that's on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a report from the intelligence administration, part of which you were, to the president, Mr. Izetbegovic, a report that was sent to him. And we see in lines 19, 20, 21, and 22 -- could you please indicate the lines to assist the witness. This is in the fourth paragraph and it says: "In preparations for a future operation to link up the enclaves, we brought in and took back four brigade commanders, two brigade chiefs of staff and the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division. The division commander who was meant to go on the next helicopter flight did not return." My question, Witness, is: Is this a document from your intelligence administration, because you told us yesterday that you were part of that administration, and was this document sent to President Izetbegovic and does it refer to activities that I've just read out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate your question, but you have to understand that this is the first time that I see this document and how could I know what it says here about some events and communication written by the brigade general or Brigadier-General Talijan. I had nothing to do with this. My combat was a non-combat unit. Our task was just to gather intelligence and forward it. We never were informed of anything that is contained in this information, nor was such information sent to us. You should ask commanders or chiefs of units, but not us. Because I really have nothing to do with this. I've never heard or seen this document in my entire life. Perhaps the chief of department would be the right person to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I didn't ask you whether you have ever seen or heard of this document. My question, like the ones -- the previous ones, was whether you knew anything about these activities which were being discussed by the commanders in Zepa and Srebrenica before the fall of Srebrenica because they were part of your command. And I was just asking you whether you knew about their activities. I wasn't asking you about this very document, nor was it my intention to tender it through you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will answer for the last time this type of question. I really don't know anything about these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 1D31, page 1 -- oh, that's the document we already have. All right. Could we then see, please, 1D32. 1D32.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, that's Exhibit D16.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see this document on the monitor, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now I will read the first sentence of this document to you. "According to intelligence information," and I repeat, "according to intelligence information, the aggressor is grouping forces and equipment around the demilitarised zones of Srebrenica and Zepa, particularly in the sector of Milici and Vlasenica." This was drafted on the 17th of February, 1995. Did you participate in the gathering of this intelligence information? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell me where you worked and what you did up until the 17th of February, 1995, what unit were you in and what military structure did you belong to? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go into private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was my intention as well. Private, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I thought we were in open session. I don't have anything to hide. I don't know why we were in private session. Let me ask the witness this:

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say that you know nothing of the order. Had you ever received the order, and it lists among the addressees, the 2nd Corps command, the command of OG Srebrenica, and the command of the Zepa Brigade, and you being part of the corps must have fallen under these categories?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if such an order ever arrived and if it did, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up 1D -- or rather D1, page 8. In Serbian, line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And which page in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's page 9 in English, but I don't know. I don't speak English. I think it's page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps your legal advisor can help you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is page 9 in English, line 21. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to page 1 in Serbian, or rather, page 8. Page 8 in Serbian and page 10 in English. I can't read it for the witness. Can we go one page back in Serbian, please. Once again, can we have page 9 in Serbian, and that's two pages ahead of the one we have now. This is page 24 in e-court. Can we go on to page 26. Thank you. I will now quote. "Pursuant to a decision issued by the commander of the 285th Brigade" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, excuse me, but could you please indicate where you are reading. It is a page full of sentences. If the witness should follow what you are quoting, you should indicate which line it is and if we have the right page in English, otherwise it's not feasible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm reading from line 21, which reads -- I don't know if -- if you can see it, but it says: "On the decision of the commander of the 285th Brigade" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please indicate with the cursor line 21, which starts with the words: "Commander, 285th Brigade ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, and if we look at the line above, at the end of that line you will see the start of the sentence which goes as follows: "On the order of the commander of the 285th Brigade, nine groups were formed which performed these tasks. These groups engaged in combat and destroyed around 60 Chetniks, and a group went into the village of Visnjica and set alight several homes. On the return from the area of Zepa of the sabotage platoons in the area of Srebrenica and further afield, activities aimed at raising the combat-readiness were taken." My question is as follows: This order given by the commander to the Srebrenica units to engage in sabotage activities in the rear of the VRS units and around Serbian villages, did it result in the death of some 60 individuals and did it have to do with the intelligence you may have gathered about the activities of the VRS in and around enclaves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat what I've already said. This is the first time I see this document. It looks like an interesting read, reads like a novel, but I've never seen this document before, I've never heard of these events before, and I think that asking me to give an opinion on this is pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If activities are carried out around the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, is it not logical for the forces in Zepa and Srebrenica to engage -- is it logical for them, that is, to engage in sabotage activities outside of their enclaves rather than attempt and protect the area within?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't get your question. I don't see what it is that I have to say. I wasn't specialised in this sort of operational activity, I wasn't a commander, I don't see what it has to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, Witness, it has to do with your activities. You furnished your commander with intensifying activities of VRS in and around the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. As a result, the commander issued an order whereby combat-readiness was to be raised and sabotage activities were to be undertaken, which in fact resulted in the death of 60 individuals in and around demilitarised zones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Were these activities and the loss of life the result of the intelligence they furnished to -- their commander with as a result of which he issued this order? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that your statement is true insofar it states that we handed over the intelligence we had to the assistant commander for intelligence, and he in turn gave them to the commander. Now, all the rest, which orders followed and which activities followed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I know, Witness, that you did not take part in these activities, but you did take part in gathering intelligence about the activities of VRS. And was it necessary to report on intensified activities of the VRS in February when there were none and was this done, in fact, just to engage in sabotage activities in the VRS-controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can never give a yes or no answer to questions that are this complex. The answer may be yes and the answer may be no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, on the first day of the examination-in-chief, in answer to Judge Mindua's question, you said that you knew nothing of the air-lift. Do you recall that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was your answer that you didn't know anything about the air-lift?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had no idea, and I do still say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see a document yesterday which had to do with the air-lift, and it was not admitted into evidence, where the commander of Zepa and Srebrenica said that even vagabonds were aware of the plan to link up Zepa and Srebrenica with the AOR of the corps and that he wanted to change the axis from Srebrenica to Zepa? Were you the only one then who were not informed, unlike all the other ones in the enclave who knew that such a plan was in the making? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I object to the question. It's argumentative, first of all; and secondly, it misstates what the document actually said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In your line of questions, Mr. Tolimir, there's a problem. There are many, many statements instead of questions. Sometimes you ask a question at the end if that is right what you are stating, but you should really ask questions to the witness. It is much more helpful for your defence. Could you please rephrase your last question to enable the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My question for the witness is as follows: Did he give in answer to my questions today the same answers that he gave to Judge Mindua's question when he asked him about whether he knew about the air-lifts or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This question was already answered, that he stood by that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we call up Prosecution 65 ter document 3. This is the agreement on demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, that's Exhibit D21.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please look at Article 1, where it is stated: "Demilitarised area will include the territory -- so the demilitarised area will include the area within the current lines of conflict. The precise boundaries will be marked by the UNPROFOR commander on the ground after consultations." This is my question: Witness, was the area within the lines of conflict in Srebrenica demilitarised, based on the intelligence you gathered? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that I've seen now for the first time and I can't tell you whether Srebrenica was demilitarised or not. If I have to give an answer, then it will be: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. My question was as follows: Did you have this knowledge from the intercepts that your unit made?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the question put a moment ago had to do with 1993, and now we've skipped to 1995. I would kindly ask you, as a senior officer, to stick to one period. It's been 17 years and it's very difficult for me to remember all these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Please tell us, based on the intelligence you gathered, both in 1993 and in 1995, was Srebrenica a demilitarised zone or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this agreement, it should have been, but our main task was to collect intelligence information about the enemy, and the enemy, in order for them to carry out normal activities and to keep their units there, the enemy would say no. I wasn't in Srebrenica, so I can't answer your question. I know that the Army of Republika Srpska was well armed and that they held positions around Srebrenica. Now, as to what the people inside the town had, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Tell me, please, did you intercept communications of your army at all, and did you in the intercepted conversations of the officers of the VRS hear anything about the status of the army, about combat groups, sabotages, infiltration of weapons in Srebrenica in the enclave itself? Did you hear anything about it at all? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in that unit, we never intercepted conversations of the BH army for the simple reason that the BH army did not have radio relay communications. It was mostly wire, fixed communications, and package radio. Right now I would probably be best placed to answer your questions if I took reports from 1995 and if I read them. So if I were to read some reports from the period of time that you're referring to, perhaps I could give some answer to your question; as it is, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to avoid you reading documents now, would you please tell us whether Srebrenica and Zepa were demilitarised, and can a zone in which there's more than 6.000 armed soldiers be ever considered to be a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot answer that question. If the zone was indeed demilitarised, as is stipulated in the agreement, then there shouldn't be any armed soldiers there and there shouldn't be any soldiers around the demilitarised zone. But since I never visited Srebrenica, it's pointless for me to continue answering this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Would you please tell us what forces, then, could have carried out this sabotage operation and killed 60 people if these forces were not armed? Could this have been done by civilians? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think the witness has gone over this a couple of different ways and I think the witness has already answered the question in about 50 different ways. What the question now put to the witness calls for is just rank speculation, since the witness has said he doesn't know anything specifically about these events or the units that were involved in it, or how it was ordered or planned or carried out, if at all. So I object to the question on that basis, and I think it might be more appropriate to move to a different area of examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think that was a good advice by Mr. Vanderpuye. Really, your last question was pure speculation. Everybody could answer that in that way. He wants to do that but it is not helpful to find out the truth what happened at that time really. Please carry on and perhaps move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D151 -- I apologise. Could we now see 1D151, page 5, lines 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm told that this document is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since the document is not in e-court and I wanted to show it to the witness, can I nevertheless put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And my question is: Do you know that General Delic, as the army commander, informed the public, the general public, that there was a plan to connect Zepa and Srebrenica with Tuzla and that that plan was in the hands of the commanders of Zepa and Srebrenica and the commander of your corps? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that General Delic after the fall of Zepa and Srebrenica spoke at a session of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, saying that there was a plan to link-up the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica with the 2nd Corps and that the commanders of Zepa and Srebrenica had the plan in their hands. Are you aware of this, given that this speech of his at the Assembly was carried in the media and there were numerous comments and a lot of discontent was caused by the statement of his? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't hear this statement of his. Now, whether I know of how dissatisfied and bitter the people were, because a lot of them had come into the area where we lived, then yes, I am aware of that. I saw it with my own eyes and it had nothing to do with the army. These people were embittered and it was normal because there were mothers who came with children and there were wounded, elderly people there, and then several thousand people were gone, were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Did the intelligence service come up with an intelligence game where they were showing to the command staff that Zepa and Srebrenica were endangered while at the same time they were covering Zepa and Srebrenica with an air-lift by using this intelligence information as a pretext? We saw that in one of the documents that was on the screen, where they were saying that they used the intelligence information as a cover-up? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about such games. But from a human point of view, if so many people are put in such a confined area, then nothing good will come out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, was it to be expected that these people from Zepa and Srebrenica tended to link up with Tuzla and conduct such offensive operations that they, in fact, did eventually conduct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was war time. Since both you and I studied the Geneva Conventions and its provisions, the normal thing would have been to release these people and there would have been nothing for you and me to discuss today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm satisfied with your answers. We will now turn to another group of questions which pertain to your testimony in-chief where you spoke about intercepting communications. And on page 2187, line 28 [as interpreted], and 2188, line 4 of the transcript of this case, you said as follows, I'm quoting: "If intercepted conversations were recorded and the tape contained four hours of intercepts or more, than these tapes would be taken to the corps command where the EDA would play them, re-record the important intercepts, erase everything else, and send the tape back." Do you remember saying this to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, while the tapes were carried to be re-recorded, how long did it take to re-record them and do what you describe here?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to thank you because this is a topic that I'm familiar with and I can actually give you some answers. Whenever the shifts finished their work, they would take the full tapes containing recordings and in exchange they would give empty tapes. And that would be taken to the command of the 2nd Corps. The shifts lasted ten days. They rotated every ten days. They would listen to these recordings, re-evaluate them, and I'm telling you this based on what I know. I never participated in this, but I know what they were saying, that they would re-listen, re-record important conversations, and then erase. Sometimes it would happen that they would forget to erase what wasn't needed and then we would have to do that. So these shifts stayed at the command of the 2nd Corps for ten days. The rotations were ten days long and this, what I said, pertained to the tapes both from the south location and the north location. And these teams would stay at the corps command for ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any situations where you had nothing to record intercepts with because you had no tapes and you didn't have them because the tapes would stay at the corps command for ten days?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be open enough and tell you that, yes, we had such instances too. And then we would use our own judgement to erase some intercepts to have sufficient space on tape to record new ones. The proper way to do it would be to keep everything on tapes, and as I have said yesterday, we used the experience of the JNA, where tapes would be taken to the analysis department, they would keep what they needed, erase everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any situations where intercepted conversations would be just jotted down on paper and not recorded because you had no space on tapes?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we had no such instances for the simple reason that one can remember a maximum of two sentences perhaps and not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you receive notebooks for your unit for the first time? You spoke here on page 4521851, lines 19 to 28, you say: "We did not have enough food, let alone notebooks. They did not appear until 1995." Did you receive, then, notebooks in 1995; and if so, in which month? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stated this. Except for our own resourcefulness and our own efforts to find notebooks wherever we could, we started receiving notebooks from the logistics department of the corps command. We wrote reports on various forms. The main problem up until period of time was that we did not have an obligation to save these notebooks. In order to keep better records, I and the people who worked with me decided that every document, incoming and outgoing, had to be recorded regardless on the type of the form and the size of the notebooks, whether it was A4 or A5. We also had loose sheets of paper that we used. So the improvement that we introduced was that we would record the exact time, the exact frequency, and we would also record the existence of the document. And this is something that had been done prior to this, except that there was no duty to keep, to save, documents and records. Up until that time, the only document that was important was the typed-up document. Once a document was typed up and was assigned a number that was put in the heading, then only that document was to be kept and preserved. That was the only duty we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Could you tell us, was it standard practice in the JNA that all the intercepts had to be destroyed as well as the notebooks if anything was written down on them because at that time they were not recognised as evidence in court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that based on my experience I shouldn't even try to answer that question. This had to do with state relations, and you very well know how such relations are regulated. And, Your Honour, I believe that this is no place or time to answer a question like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You don't have to answer me, but answer the Trial Chamber. Do you know whether in the former Yugoslavia a tape, a reel-to-reel tape, could ever be used as an exhibit in trial proceedings before a court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could we judge another state and use materials in our own state that under the then-international agreements and conventions were not allowed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, I doubt if your position is correct. You were asked by the accused: "Could you tell us, was it standard practice in the JNA that all the intercepts had to be destroyed as well as notebooks if anything was written down on them because at that time they were not recognised as evidence in court?" If you focus on the first part of this question, was that standard practice? That has nothing to do with the relations between states. You should answer that question. Was it standard practice in the JNA that all the intercepts had to be destroyed as well as the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there were clear tasks for people at my level and clear instructions as to what types of documents could be kept and which not. Some had to be kept permanently, some, such as personnel files, were kept for a certain number of years. But again, I would like to reiterate, this was peace time. There was no war going on, so there was no need for this type of work. And that is why I said that maybe this is not the place or the time for me to talk about these things. Maybe I misspoke, but in my own experience I never had occasion to have something that I wrote down or a tape be -- is used in a court of law. I know very well that in democratic countries, such as the United States, for instance, without a court order you could not seize anything or use it. However, during war time, the situation is completely different. We -- I mean, to have a court order so as to be able to defend oneself and intercept, that's a completely different situation to the situation as it was before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps there was a misunderstanding. That was not the question. The question was if it happened that if it was the normal practice to destroy notebooks and tapes at the relevant time we're talking about. Could you focus on that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said it was standard practice for certain documents to be kept for a certain period of time. How long that period would be and what type of documents, I really don't know, but I know that some documents had to be kept for two years, three, five, ten years, and some of them were to be kept forever. But I was not a person who had any responsibilities in that, so I really didn't know. I just produced the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wasn't -- it wasn't my intention to discuss political issues with the witness. But let me ask the witness this:

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was Mustafa Hajrulahovic, was he a person who would know or order you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would request the accused to repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. The interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, tell us, please, did General Mustafa Hajrulahovic, was he informed about your practice of destroying notebooks and of the fact that you had a shortage of the necessary equipment and materials for taping intercepts? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the gentleman, who is now late, was informed or not, but I know that when I arrived at the unit it was not standard practice to keep those log-books. For a simple reason that you cannot ask someone to keep something unless they actually issued that to you. So all these different notebooks and log-books we brought with us when we came there because there was no standard issue. I know that in peace time it's done differently. You would go to the quartermasters and get whatever you need, but at this time we had nothing. So the only thing that we had to keep were the documents that had a stamp on them with the number and date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is that a convenient time to have the first break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have the first break now on technical reasons and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness and then, Mr. Tolimir, you may continue. Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. At page 28, lines 12 to 17, of the transcript you stated, among other things, that there was no duty to keep, to save documents and records. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: That being the case, what was the criteria that was used to determine what to keep and what not to keep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said, when I arrived at the unit which had operated in the way it had because these were not professional soldiers, they had no equipment, no documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's no interpretation in the B/C/S, I think, especially there's no direct connection to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can hear you, but I was not receiving any interpretation. But it's just now that we do have the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We try to carry on. Please carry on with your answer. I have interrupted you because of the technical problems. Perhaps it is solved in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the Bosnian army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's still -- wait a moment. It should be okay now. Excuse me, please repeat again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One, two, three. One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now please again repeat the -- your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that the BH army was composed of non-professionals, or rather, people, normal, regular people. So when I arrived there, there was a need to bring some order to all that. In my statement I said that these notebooks as well as some others that were not marked were preserved by chance. That's how fate would have it. As for when I arrived in the unit, I felt the need to bring some order in there because it was already the third year of the war. We needed to get the maximum out of our people, and you will certainly know that we had no idea what would happen in July - and I'm referring to the period February -- January, February 1995. So that as for the keeping of the documents, there arose the need to keep them for a certain period of time. And I can say that all the printed documents that had a heading and stamp on it were handed over to the depots. And when the Tribunal arrived, we did not really know what it was they were looking for and what it was they needed. And then as we worked together and in conversations, we learned or it was learned that these notebooks were still in existence. They wanted to see them, and when they did they said that was exactly what they needed. And that was how those notebooks found their way here. And I'm not saying -- or rather, what I'm saying is there are many notebooks from the previous, earlier, period but many of them had been burnt. And when I arrived there, I insisted on reports being made and these reports would have a heading and a stamp and a number assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Earlier, Witness, we left off with a question about the procurement of these notebooks that Judge Nyambe was referring to. I asked you how it was possible - and that's what I would like to ask you now -- so how was it possible that you exchanged all kinds of different materials for notebooks and that you did not receive notebooks, and that your chief, your immediate superior and his superior, did not know that you did not have -- that there was a shortage of these materials that you needed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know if my superior up the chain of command in Sarajevo knew of the shortage of material. We had to have tapes because they were the key to our work. Without magnetic tapes, we would not be able to have recordings of intelligence. We wouldn't have been able to preserve the substance of these intercepts. I recall very well that in the summer we went through a period of crisis because of the shortages. We particularly had a shortage of food, and for a period of 15 days we would rely on the mushrooms that were growing nearby and we had them for our meals. They are very nutritious. And in this way we were able to set aside some resources to buy notebooks. You will know, of course, that whatever could be spared was sent to the front lines. Notebooks were the last thing that senior officers and commanders would be concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that -- don't you find it odd that you, being such an important structure, had to get by on mushrooms and had to rely on your own resourcefulness to obtain notebooks, whilst your government in Sarajevo was spending millions? Don't you find that a bit odd, in view of the importance of your unit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how many millions the government in Sarajevo had or how much it spent. What I do know is that we were toward the lower end of the scale when it came to our importance, regardless of the role that we played. Apparently other things were considered to be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know if audio recordings of intercepts which were adduced as evidence in this case had been preserved as well? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we discussed this yesterday when we talked about the various reports and records. My opinion is - which I cannot confirm with 100 per cent certainty - is that some of these audio recordings can be found in the central archives in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us why there isn't a single notebook to be found here which does not have the labels on them that the Prosecution showed here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would prefer to have first the question if the witness is able to answer the -- to hear the answer to the question if the witness is able to give the answer, and then you might raise something. Witness, could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there should be such notebooks. We saw yesterday in the documents that we had notebooks of A5 size and A4 size, some of them with multi-colour covers. And I know that such notebooks were handed over to the Prosecution. Now, why they haven't found their way here is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The last part of the witness's answer is the reason why I was objecting to the question, is that he wouldn't know what's in evidence and not in evidence before the Court. But I think it's clear on the record what the disposition of those notebooks are. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I think the Chamber's of the view that this witness is able to deal with the different kinds of questions. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I put my question because in the course of the examination-in-chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on with your questioning. It's not necessary to explain anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- what was shown and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please just carry on with your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we call up 1D128, page 47, paragraph 3. 1D128. Can we have a look at paragraph 3 on the right-hand side, and I will read it for the witness. It's in English. Again, it's the book that we showed the witness yesterday. I'm quoting the words of the author of the book. "The many intercepts that were later published and disclosed at the trial of General Krstic give the impression that the VRS troop movements were efficiently followed by the Muslims in real time. There were dozens of intercepts which showed that the ABiH interception stations at the" northern and southern locations "closely followed the VRS conversations about the column heading for Tuzla. However, at Krstic's trial no attention was paid to whether this intelligence was shared with UNPROFOR. This would, after all, have been a logical step, given that the Bosnian Muslims dearly wanted to get UNPROFOR or NATO on their side in the fight against the VRS."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I have read out a portion of the analysis on Srebrenica and Zepa conducted by the Dutch institute. This is my question: You were involved in the hand-over of documentation to the Prosecution, as we were able to see yesterday. Were you ever in the course of the war involved in the hand-over of intercepts to UNPROFOR or NATO or was anyone from your service involved in it?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, either during the war or after the war did I hand over anything to UNPROFOR or NATO. Now, did anyone from the command do this and on what basis is something I can't tell. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be logical to divert the attention of NATO, having been sought to strike upon the VRS forces, since as you indicated yesterday, as we were able to see yesterday, the intelligence in the gathering of which you were involved happened -- was gathered in real time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will state again, because it's the case and that was the situation, the intelligence was gathered in real time. We were the producers of intelligence. Now, the path from there on to the corps command, who was involved in this process, is something I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On the first day we were able to see only a list of documents or notebooks handed over to the Prosecution. This is my question: Does there exist a list of documents containing the intercepts that you delivered to your superiors in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat what I said. The process of recording outgoing telegrams takes place in such a way that there would be a log-book of incoming and outgoing telegrams where it would be noted. Now, the communications centre which received telegrams would also have a log-book of incoming and outgoing telegrams because what I was referring to was the intelligence network. I don't know what happened of these log-books, but I believe that all of them were handed over to Sarajevo in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, I think you understand why I put this question. If you have a list of documents that you handed over to the Prosecution, do you, by the same token, have a list of documents as they were sent to the end users in the corps and in the army? Would you have such a log-book with such entries kept in the central archives in Sarajevo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question fully. What I'm saying is related to the time-period of which I have knowledge. We had a log-book of outgoing telegrams, a log-book of incoming telegrams, and you would have the code-name of a given telegram, the exact time, and every midnight all the stations would compare the number of telegrams sent out and received and match them. Now, what happened with those log-books, I'm not claiming that all of them were handed over to Sarajevo. What has become of them, where are they today, do they still exist or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Can you tell us the following: When was the first time that the intelligence contained in the intercepts you commented on in this trial and in the Krstic trial was made available to your government or to your army in general?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I'm not sure whether it was first the representatives of the ICTY or the NIOD that came first, and whatever we did, we did on the orders of the command concerned. They took statements, and then afterwards, ICTY representatives came up. They were asking for information concerning the name you mentioned in your question. In those early days, the information sought directly concerned the gentleman named above. At first individual reports were provided, and at a later stage everything that could be found in the archive of the 2nd Corps or the intelligence department of the 2nd Corps at that point in time was taken. As for the rest, I can't talk about it. Was this something that I was specifically told? I don't know. I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Is my understanding of what you said correct? For the first -- the first time that these intercepts became a matter of interest was when the representatives of the Dutch institute showed up, the NIOD, and representatives of the ICTY, and that was in the matter of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's clarify this. NIOD representatives were not specifically interested in either the general - and I'm referring to General Krstic - or in intercepts. If I remember correctly, they wanted to get a view of the situation from the participants in the war. My superior wanted me to say something from the perspective of the interception of certain communications. And as for the others, I don't know. I know of my superior. I think there was the corps commander as well. I am not familiar with these other names mentioned here. NIOD representatives left after talking to me. I don't know if they said anything to my superior. They didn't tell me anything other than asked me to give them precise answers to their questions. They were never specifically asking for information concerning General Krstic. They never even mentioned him. As far as I know, the first time that ICTY representatives -- it was only when the ICTY representatives came that they were interested in General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And a moment ago you said that your boss approved your conversation with representatives of the NIOD and the ICTY. Could you tell us what year this was, was this your boss during the war time or your boss later on when this was happening? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you is this: We gave a statement. I may be mistaken in the date or the year, but I believe it was 1998. But please don't take my word for it. My boss was the one who handed over the documents. And as for 1995, who my boss was then, I can't really recall because they changed all the time, almost every six months or every year there would be a new person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So we have now established that these were your bosses from 1998, so we cannot confuse that with 1995. So this was in 1998. Have I understood you correctly, that boss? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad, sir, that you got it, but in 1998, or rather, in 1997 and 1998 there were two different departments within the corps, security and intelligence. And there were assistant commanders for security and the other one was also an assistant commander and an assistant commander for intelligence. In 1998 I returned to the corps command, and these two departments were now combined into one G2 according to NATO standards and a certain number of individuals then were to be in that one department. And one of them who signed the notes, he became the boss of G2, the head of G2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Could you tell us, please, whether up until 1998 any after your superiors, either at the intelligence department or within the command chain, did anyone ask any information from you regarding the contents of the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to any specific time-frame or are you talking about the ongoing developments?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I was really referring to the period from since the war ended up until 1998. Did anyone ask you to provide information about the contents of those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't asked by anyone for such information, but let me clarify this. The intercepts or the surveillance continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that. I was just asking about the documents that we are discussing now. Witness, tell us, please, did any of your superiors ever at the army level have contacts with foreign representatives, either UNPROFOR or NATO or a NATO member country? Did any of your superiors ever forward to them intelligence data that your service collected during the war?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know whether anyone sent information, but as far as I recall, within the corps command there was a department that liaised with UNPROFOR. That's all I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this liaison department with UNPROFOR, did they have access to your information and did anyone else have access to your -- to the information or intelligence that you had? Because you said it was handed -- up until when it was handed over to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if anyone had access. I'm just saying that all the material from -- all these materials were archived in early 1996 and our work continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time when he was the chief of the security department, could you tell me -- and I'm referring to Hajrulahovic and after him, in other words, during the period of his successor, was any of your intelligence data used by any of the international factors, the UNPROFOR, NATO, or any NATO member states and so on, any of those who were in charge of monitoring the situation in the former Yugoslavia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what information was used in the negotiations, but as for the general you mentioned, I only know that he passed away. I never had any personal contacts with him. All I know is that he held this post during the -- in the early years of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to read out the next sentence in this paragraph, the words of Rupert Smith, and I mean Rupert Smith who is the commander of UNPROFOR during the events that we are discussing here and which are the subject matter of these proceedings. He says the following: "Smith's door was always open to the head of the Bosnian intelligence service, General Mustafa Hajrulahovic but he never dropped by. On the other hand, the ABiH army had excellent intelligence contacts with the Americans." That's in the last paragraph. You can see and recognise the words. You can recognise the name, Smith, and -- thank you. Does this mean that representatives of the UN who are supposed to report to the Security Council about -- on the situation in the field never forwarded to your service any information that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really had no dealings and nothing to do with the things that are described here in this book, and I believe that you are just confusing the levels. I was never at this level. I didn't know any of these people. I wasn't even in Sarajevo during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As an intelligence officer, do you know whether your superiors from the intelligence department shared their intelligence with the American intelligence services? Do you know anything about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever told me nor did I know anything about what they shared and with whom. If that did happen, this would have had to be done at a higher level. At my level, these things did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D128, please, page 18. This is the e-court number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Dissemination of intercepted signals is always accompanied by great secrecy. The exchange of comment in particular is very limited. Only a small circle of the highest political and military policy makers are given access to this. This secrecy is also important when it comes to sharing intelligence between the United States and its allies. The British foreign secretary, Malcolm Rifkind is reported to have resisted the release of intercepts made by the GC headquarters which the NSA wanted to hand over to the Yugoslavia Tribunal in support of the prosecution of Slobodan Milosevic. At the end of 1996, the Clinton administration was prepared to release intercepts for this purpose, but once again the British government blocked the process." [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: From this quotation we can see what we already know, that such communications are held as very -- or confidential, in the highest secrecy. Now, can you tell me who else had access other than you and the people who actually processed them? Could you tell us who other than you had access to them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you that access to raw intelligence was allowed to people who actually analysed them, the command, the superior command, and then they sent it to their superior command in Sarajevo. Now, who the people were who had access to them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: you ever prohibited in 1994 and 1995 from meeting certain individuals or to travel abroad? Did anyone ever impose such restrictions on you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, during the war I didn't travel anywhere -- abroad nor any of my men, that's one. Two, there were restrictions and there was a ban even after the war on these activities. We could not do this without the approval of the competent command. And as for these other things, I really don't know what to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just ask for a redaction in the transcript at page 45, line 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be done. Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, when was it first that you heard -- what year did you hear for the first time that documents have to be handed over to the ICTY, the OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor, and when was -- when did your superiors ask of you to do this for the first time?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, this happened for the first time in the spring of 1998. That's approximately the same time, the time of the first reports. In other words, it could have been a few weeks or days earlier or later, but in any case in spring of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Tell us, please, at your level and in your department, did you know that other services, too, were engaged in collecting intelligence and they -- and that they, too, could document the same events that you did? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which other services you are specifically referring to, but in -- when the -- when in 1998 the security and intelligence departments were merged, of course there was intelligence from the security department. For instance, the reports or notes that I discussed yesterday where I said that I hadn't seen them before. So these were the types of documents, and also I know about these other two individuals who worked with us together at the location, at the facilities, where we monitored the work. As for the others, I don't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So for the most part, all those materials, including the intercepts that are under discussion here, had to go through your hands, through the department and your men, they all had to be registered in your department, yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that these were materials that we had handed over. As for whether there were other documents collected from elsewhere, you should ask those different departments or individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is what you know or knew about your army. And now I would like to ask you about other armies. Do you know that other armies too could intercept and tape conversations and information in the areas referred to here in these intercepts used as evidence before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I know that there were some departments in the Army of Republika Srpska and the Yugoslav Army. As for the others, I really don't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Republika Srpska army, was it capable and was it able to intercept and monitor conversations in the same manner that you were? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I think that they did have the capabilities, but I've already said here that our system of packet communications and cryptographic encoding were done and I don't know how it was done in the Republika Srpska army. And at this point in time I don't know how they operate because the technologies have changed and now most of the work is done through analogue systems and digital -- actually, there was a transition from the analogue to the digital system, and how it's being done now I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether foreign services other than the services of the former Yugoslav republics, for instance, NATO states such as the United States, Britain, and so on, did you know that they monitored all communications in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether they had all of this under their control, as you're saying. But I know that they did control us in the physical sense. They controlled personnel, ammunition, units, facilities, and so on. It was their permanent task.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D128, page 13, in e-court. 230 and 231 are the page numbers of the book. And this is a book by the Dutch institute and it's about Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But let me ask you first: Do you know that the United States had a so-called mercury satellite which was capable of intercepting even radio communications on talkie-walkies and similar equipment?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the existence of that satellite. I don't know what it was used for. Now, whether they used their satellites in the territory of Bosnia, I don't know. We had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the CIA director John Deutch came to Republika Srpska and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1996 when he was the CIA director and that he officially confirmed that there had been satellites for intercepting communications?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly regret, but I neither know John Deutch nor do I know that in 1996 he came for a visit and what he said on that occasion. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is on the left side, first paragraph, second sentence -- I apologise, on the right side. This is the right side. It doesn't say here that he came to visit Republika Srpska, but the other things I said about his visit you can find that in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I know we've gone around on this topic for quite some time, but I don't see what the relevance is of the questions that Mr. Tolimir's putting to the witness. I don't see what the relevance is of this witness's knowledge of the capacity of other entities to intercept -- I don't see what that has to do with either the accuracy, reliability, or the ability of the ABiH army to intercept VRS communications. And so either I would ask Mr. Tolimir to either clarify the basis of it, otherwise I just don't see how this is relevant to the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber would appreciate if you could focus on that part of the evidence of the witness he can really testify about. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have an intelligence officer testifying here who also acted as an advisor to the OTP on the same topic that we are discussing here. This is why I've been putting these questions to him here. And I even asked him whether he would act as their advisor in my case as well. This is why I'm putting these questions to him. I think that as an officer he should be able to answer this, and I always lay the foundation for my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you realise what the witness was able to answer. Please carry on but focus on his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know that the drones and also various aircraft, manned and unmanned, was used to intercept communications in the conflict that we are dealing with in this Tribunal, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the NATO centre for air operations with its headquarter in Vicenza, in Italy, which co-ordinated all air operations over Bosnia was also involved in intercepting communications? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The majority of the notebooks whose cover we saw here in your evidence in-chief, was it manufactured in Italy?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that and this is the first time that I hear such a question. I never paid attention to where the notebooks were from. It was important for us to simply have notebooks. We didn't care where they had been manufactured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And can you tell us where you obtained these notebooks? The OTP showed us on the screen a number of these notebooks containing intercept records, and almost all of these notebooks, up to the number of 48, were all manufactured in Italy, save for three or four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is the question, Mr. Tolimir? You've got the answer already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness said that he heard it for the first time so I simply reminded him, and my question comes now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Put -- please put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D136, please. Thank you. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what we see on our screens, is it notebook 84? It says "84" over this picture.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this notebook from the collection of notebooks containing intercepts made by your unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 2 of this notebook. And the witness can now tell us whether this document comes from his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you conclude based on this that this document comes from the facility mentioned here as the facility north in this case?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it looks like, like a notebook from the northern facility.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 1 of this document, 1D136. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You intercepted communications in 1995. How do you then explain that in the upper corner it says in Italian: "ID." And then it says "Italian university." And the date is the 1st of January, 2001. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know and I don't know what this stands for, "1 GEN 2001," I don't know. This notebook definitely is from 1995. And I have no explanation.
