utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, if it is from 1995, how come it says here on this notebook "1st generation 2001"?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain what is written here, but how do you think that I could have handed over this notebook to the OTP representatives in 1998 with this date, 2001, written on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Everything is odd concerning this, but one could ask whether this notebook was created in 1995 or perhaps in a later period of time.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm testifying under oath here and I'm certain that all notebooks that we handed over to the OTP representatives come from 1995 or earlier period of time. They were created when the intercepts were recorded in the southern and northern facility in time up to 1995, and how this writing came to be on the notebook I have no idea. It could have been done later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we ask the Trial Chamber to request the OTP to produce the original notebook so that all of us here can see that we didn't put this stamp on the notebook. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's no problem. I believe we can have the notebook available for Mr. Tolimir to inspect if he'd like. Again, I believe Mr. Gajic has had an opportunity to view it as well. But I would object to the line of questioning all together, and the reason for that is, I would ask Mr. Tolimir, rather, to proffer a good-faith basis for putting a question to the witness that the book was manufactured in 2001, because as you can see from the exhibit before you, there is nothing put fictitious writing on the cover of this book. It's -- there's a photograph there of a chipmunk with a University of Italia T-shirt on. It purports to be an identity card of this chipmunk. It's signed by the mayor in Sindaco, it says, of Popotiucci, which are completely fictitious characters' names and numbers on this book. So -- and it says the signature of the chipmunk on the identity card as "Popotia," it says. So I would ask Mr. Tolimir to put or to come forward with a good-faith basis for the line of questioning to suggest that this book was manufactured at a time other than what the witness says. Otherwise I don't think it's a relevant line of questioning. But of course, as I said, I'll be happy to make this book available to the Trial Chamber and to anybody else who would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, this problem could have been raised in re-examination, but I would like to clarify to shorten this kind of question, I would like to ask the witness: Can you tell me which parts of this cover page of this notebook were produced by you or members of your unit? What you can see here on the screen, is there anything or what was written down or in other way produced on this page by you or members of your unit? Do we have a problem with the transcript? Thank you. I was told we have a problem with record on LiveNote, but it is covered fully. Thank you. Do you remember my question? Could you explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is how it was. Underneath "Carta Di Identita Dei Popoti," it says "Number 14, log-book of notes 4," and then the designation of the piece of equipment, 100 plus 450B, that's what the members of our unit wrote. And then over the picture you can see number 84, if I'm not mistaken. We wrote that number together with the OTP representatives in 1998, and you can probably find this notebook under number 84 in the record which was made when the documents were handed over. I'm not 100 per cent sure, but I'm pretty confident that this notebook would be found under number 84 in the hand-over record. That's all that we wrote. As for the rest of the text, I don't know about it. I'm actually convinced now that this notebook can be found under number 84 in the record made in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on. We have now the explanation you wanted to have. Please carry on -- one question by Judge Nyambe. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just a clarification from the witness. Looking at the document on the screen, there is a number "1 GEN 2001." You can see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Here is the question: At the time you used -- at the time this notebook was used by you or somebody in your department, was that number on the notebook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't make any statements in relation to the part of the text which says "1 GEN 2001," but I can definitely tell you that the number that we have there, which is 00789467, was not written there before 1998. And I'm also sure that this large number written in a marker was not written before either. And I'm sure that this document can be found among the 135 documents that we handed over. That part I'm sure of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I owe you an explanation for my request to show -- to have this shown again. The witness said that this particular stamp, "1 GEN 2001," may have been placed there subsequently. And I said that this document was constantly within the chain of custody of the Prosecution. And I'm reiterating my request for the original notebook to be shown to the witness. The Defence could not have had any part in this because we were never given the original documentation which is in the possession of the Prosecution, and we would like to tender this into evidence, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I said, I will make that notebook available for Mr. Tolimir to look at and inspect. I believe that his legal advisor has already done so. The date that's indicated on the document, 1st January 2001, on the cover of this document, purports to be the date that the chipmunk signed it. That's how fictitious the cover of this document is. That's the reason why I've asked for Mr. Tolimir to present a good-faith basis for making -- or to putting the question to the witness suggesting that the book was manufactured at a date other than what the witness has said. And he's repeatedly said that it can be found in the log, look on the second page of this notebook, as Mr. Tolimir has done, you will see a number reflected in the log-book that the witness has also just identified. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, it would be helpful to shorten the whole question of the originality of this book to have it available after the next break, and I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir to move to another topic and to leave this behind until we will have the original in the courtroom. Please carry on but not again with this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please let me know if you will receive this notebook into evidence. Secondly, a doubt was expressed here as to whether the Defence might have had a hand in this and added this or not, and that's why we would like to see the original notebook and we would like the witness to see the notebook, and then we will decide what to do on this score in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please listen to what I have said. The notebook will be available in the courtroom. Please move to another topic. We can deal with that later. And nobody said that there is a doubt that perhaps the Defence has put something on this book; nobody said that. I haven't heard it. Please carry on with another topic. We come back to this document later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we now call up again that book and page 231. That's 1D128. That's page 13 in e-court. Can we have page 17 in e-court, i.e., page 239 of the book, the headline: "Other European countries." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will quote this. It has to do with Srebrenica and Zepa. I quote: "Besides the United Kingdom, Germany, and France, other European countries also conducted Sigint operations in the former Yugoslavia. To date, almost nothing has been known about this. One known fact is that Italian monitoring stations were active during the war in Bosnia. To give one example -- to give one example, some time before the attack on the enclave the Italian monitoring service, via a monitoring station in Italy, intercepted a telephone conversation between the mayor of Srebrenica and President Izetbegovic. In this call the mayor requested permission to evacuate the population, but this was refused by Izetbegovic." And then moving on to the last line. It is also stated that the Italians had ten parabolic antennas to listen in to communications traffic in the Balkans, the Middle East, et cetera. This is my question: A moment ago we were able to see that NATO had a unit in Vicenza. We were also able to see that quite a lot of interception activities took place in Italy, hence my question. You, as an intelligence officer, did you have any knowledge of the presence of the intelligence services of Italy and their activities in intercepting communications in Zepa and Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no idea of the presence of any Italian services or centres intercepting conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the mayor of Srebrenica, as it is stated here, tried to get in touch with President Izetbegovic in order to request permission for evacuation? Was this something your service was acquainted with?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't have information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 22 in e-court now, and that's page 251 of the book on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you. We have a big problem with the transcript in LiveNote, and I was told the engineers are -- have to start the whole system again to resolve this problem. And therefore it is suggested that we have the second break now, and in the meantime this problem can be solved so that we have appropriate -- we have the record of everything is clear, but that we have both screens working sufficiently. We must have the second break now and we will resume ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if I'm not mistaken, you have -- we have not the transcript on -- the LiveNote transcript on our screen yet, but somebody will solve this problem. Mr. Tolimir, you have used more than four hours now and we should try to finish this witness today because our next hearing is Tuesday, next week, and the Prosecution must have the chance to re-examine the witness. Therefore, please carry on and try not to waste time. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, I was about to ask you another question on this book, but I'm afraid we won't have time anymore to deal with this book which addressed in great detail the issue of interception in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I'm sure you will be reading it thoroughly later as I will and everybody else. Can you tell us when did you obtain these multi-coloured notebooks that we can see on our screens now?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can tell you is that we obtained notebooks in different periods of time, different batches. At one point we also received a shipment from the corps command. But I think that this sort of notebooks appeared in early 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can I conclude, based on your answer, that these notebooks were used also during the period when the intercepts we were discussing were taken? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak about the period of early 1995 because I was there myself. I can't tell you and I don't want to make any statements in relation to the preceding period. We had small shipments, I think, previously, whereas in 1995 there were more of such notebooks to be found on the market and everywhere else. So that's how we obtained them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if there existed a different sort of notebooks which contained the intercepts recorded in manuscript which includes also the period between 10th and the 17th, which was the period we were referring to?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were other sorts of notebooks as well. You could see that we had A5-size notebooks and A4-size notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I know that there are other sorts of notebooks, but I'm asking you: Were intercepts transcribed manually in any other sorts of notebooks than the ones we were able to see and which covered the period of the 10th and the 17th July 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, most of the notebooks used in 1993 [as interpreted] looked like this. Now, whether there were other notebooks that we received from division platoons, I don't know what sort of notebooks division platoons monitoring communications used. What I do know is that most of the notebooks used for this purpose in 1995 were of this sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we find an intercept noted in a notebook which would not have been of the format that we were able to see a moment ago on our screens?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just note that in the record at page 60, line 10, it refers to notebooks being used in 1993. I think that's a transcription error, but I just wanted to clarify it for the record so that we're clear going forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please clarify. Were you referring to 1995 or 1993 in your last answer? It is written --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, I said -- sorry. I said that in 1995 most of the notebooks used were of this format. And I'm speaking of the period when I joined the unit, which doesn't mean to say that these sort of notebooks had not been used previously as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, is there an intercept relating to the critical period between 10th and the 17th which is related to these events and originates from intercepted communications of the VRS and which has not been recorded in one of these notebooks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tolimir, we had again problems with the LiveNote, but now you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My question for the witness was as follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is there a notebook where intercepts were transcribed between the period of the 10th and the 17th of July, 1995, other than the notebooks manufactured in Italy that we saw earlier on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the communications intercepted by my unit, I don't think that there are any other notebooks for the mentioned period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How do you account for the fact that only in these notebooks were the communications intercepted at all three locations and which are now the subject of this trial?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is quite a simple issue here. I think that this was the only stationery available to us, and I think the same goes for the 21st Division, the 25th Division, perhaps the 22nd as well. Ever since my arrival in the unit, in late winter or early spring, this was the sort of notebooks that we received and used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm not interested in what the other units had. Please focus on my question. My question was: Were there any other handwritten records of intercepts made in notebooks other than these, the ones that we discussed? And I'm referring to the intercepts captured by your unit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you didn't think that there should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think you have now the original notebook in your hands. The Chamber would appreciate to have the possibility to look at that as well and could the -- Mr. Vanderpuye perhaps indicate if there is any confidential material because it was shown on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the cover of the notebook, I don't believe there is, no. On the inside there is. Mr. Tolimir doesn't have the copy with him because I offered it earlier and they indicated that they didn't want it. But I have it and if the Trial Chamber would like to see it, it's certainly here. I can certainly make it available to you and I would like to make it available to you. And I don't know if Mr. Tolimir would like to see it now at this point, but it's right here on my desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We would like to see it because we dealt with that quite a long time and to clarify this topic. We would like to receive it. Court Officer, could you -- the Court Officer, could you bring it, please. Thank you. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, you said a moment ago that there were no other intercepts relating to the period between the 10th and the 17th which would have been recorded in any other notebooks. So my question is this: In the notebooks of this size, which were manufactured in Italy, were there any intercepts recorded which did not relate to the period between the 10th and the 17th?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are many such intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And do these intercepts relate to the earlier or the later period?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How much earlier were such notebooks used -- so how much in advance of the intercepts you started to make and which already related to the operations in Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can set the date from which we started using them at my arrival there, which was late February/early March. And up until November, I think you can find various intercepts recorded in such notebooks which had nothing to do with the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Fine. If these notebooks contain handwritten records of intercepts, and let's take it that these notebooks only contain intercepts relating to Srebrenica and Zepa and nothing else, was it possible for certain intercepts to have been recorded into them at a later date? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was absolutely not possible. All the notebooks were used in the facilities themselves and nothing was copied into them from any other documents. The records contained in them were the transcription directly from the communications as they were listened to on the UHER reel-to-reel tape recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So please then tell me, the intercepts that they contain, do they solely relate to Zepa and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These notebooks do not only contain intercepts related to Zepa and Srebrenica. I said that they also contain intercepts made several months ahead of that period as well as after.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we're clear on that. Can you tell me when you received these notebooks for the first time and who from? You said something about it in general terms, but I should like to know specifically.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's be quite clear. These were insignificant details at the time. As I said, we received some of the notebooks from the logistic service of the 2nd Corps. Some of the notebooks were bought in exchange for flour at the location where the unit's command was stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who did you buy the second batch of notebooks from and they are also manufactured in Italy?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the village where the unit was stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible based on the bar code present on these notebooks to determine with the manufacturer when the notebooks were produced and released to the market? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I know about it, though I don't know what the bar code specifically contains save for some information about the manufacturer, et cetera, one should be able to define whether these notebooks were manufactured in the relevant period or not. But let me tell Their Honours that the intercepts recorded in them were made in that period and that the notebooks were handed over to ICTY representatives in 1998. And that's something I stand by fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But in what way can you demonstrate that the contents of these notebooks were made back in 1995 before they were handed over to ICTY representatives for their purposes by your command?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can demonstrate it with several details, one of which is that every notebook was entered into the log-book with a designation of the military unit concerned, since the military units changed their designation numbers. Every unit would get its designation number, be it an infantry brigade or anything else, and this is something that can easily be checked through the documentation. The second detail is the handwriting which can be recognised by the individuals involved in the work, and some of the notebooks - I can't recall if all of them - I signed at the end, saying that the notebook had as many pages so as to make it impossible to add anything to it. And then thirdly, there is a log-book of all records of the unit concerned and of all the documents when they were filed, et cetera, all of this was handed over to the archives. Fourthly, all these notebooks which were filled, as soon as they were full they would be returned to the unit's command and kept in the safe. They would also be filed under certain number there. Fifthly, there were records of -- and the notebooks themselves which were taken by ICTY representatives, they were the ones to see them first, and at that time they did not contain these numbers, 84, 92, et cetera. We were supposed to sort all this documentation out and hand it over to them accompanied by a record of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You just said that the notebooks did not contain these marks at the time and that you had to jointly work on this and make a record of the hand-over, et cetera. Does it mean that you were involved in this process of placing markings?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were able to see the notebook which had number 84 on it. This was written in 1998 because it was item 84 in the record of the handover. So the only thing that was added to that notebook was number 84 which was placed in 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I call up 1D136, page 2, in order for me to be able to put a question to the witness. We'll be -- what we will soon have on our screens is page 2 of that notebook you referred to a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see it says: "Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina" at the top. You stated here yourself that you weren't able to know what was done at this level. So what strikes me as curious is that an operator should have written the name of his army there but not the title of his unit as well. How do you account for this?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, this would be written by operators working in these facilities. Whenever they had some spare time to rest they would write titles, draw lilies, as you can see them, or write "PEB." And the important thing here was to see which unit this referred to and the dates when the records were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But this is not the date when this record was made because here it says this is written by the user of this notebook. It says the student between 20th of April, 1995, up until the 9th of May, 1995. In other words, less than a month that this person was a student for 19 days. So does that mean that this notebook was actually filled for -- in a period of less than a month?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, where it says "student" and whatever's written after it, that has nothing to do with anything. What it says here is that the first intercept was recorded on the 20th April and that the last intercept was recorded on the 9th of May, 1995. This is what we insisted on. These intercepts may have come from various routes, but they were and this -- all the entries in this notebook were made from the 20th -- from those dates to that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell us, please, did you -- were you sent for training abroad other than the school you went through in the JNA during or before your centre was established?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go abroad at the time when this centre was being established. But I was sent abroad later on, after the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you were in the year 2000, what country, and was this for training or was it on private business?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I travelled to Malaysia in 2001 where I went for training. This was the basic intelligence course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you travel to any other country?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you have a passport which could corroborate what you've just told us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I really just don't see the relevance of this particular line of questioning at all. If he wants to ask him about his training, I don't see any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the accused should carry on until five minutes past half past 1.00, that means 1.35. And think about how to use this time properly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked whether the witness had a passport which would show what countries he travelled to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, when you came here to the Tribunal, did you come here with a passport? Did you have a passport with you?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When was that passport issued?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where was your last passport?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you should know that every time you're issued a new passport, the old passport is destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any of your operators go abroad for training? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, not one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We had a witness here who told us that he did go for training abroad. He was from the northern location. Is it possible that he was sent there without you knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know who this might have been, that this could have been anyone from the northern location. This could have been later on, but before 1999 -- before 1999 no one was sent abroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye -- Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again, I don't see the relevance of this line of questioning. The second thing is that the question as it was put to the witness misrepresents the record in this case because the question was asked whether or not there was anybody -- any of his unit that received the training and framed in terms of a person in a completely different unit. So I don't think it was fairly put to the witness to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could -- you have already received the answer and therefore I think we shouldn't deal with that anymore. Carry on, please, but not with the same topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could the Trial Chamber please inspect this notebook and see all the labels on it. And we would like to suggest that it be actually examined by an expert so that we could determine the time when it actually came into being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I wanted to give you the chance to finish your questioning and then the Chamber was -- intended to deal with this notebook. Perhaps first questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it possible, Witness, that entries were made in these notebooks after the fact because the intercepts were not used at the time of their actual recording? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on my experience and the way we worked, I've already told you that there was a period, a realtime period, when these reports were made and these intercepts written down that would be within an hour or two of the realtime communications and then they would be forwarded on. However, this time-frame of an hour or two was quite realistic in view of the technology that we used. And if these intercepts contained significant and urgent information, they would have been sent immediately on; and if not, they would just be recorded, taped, and then transcripts made. And I have already answered this question several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Was it standard practice to broadcast via public media transcripts of intercepts of conversations between the members of the enemy force?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the media actually broadcast and reported on conversations between General Kukanjac and some other officers from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do know about that, but I heard about this in some TV programmes after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the media report and broadcast some statements by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really wouldn't know what they reported. You have to be aware of the fact that there were power shortages, so I don't know whether they were or weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you recall whether there was an intercept of a conversation between General Mladic and Fikret Abdic broadcast in the media? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was any of your intercepts of General Mladic's conversations with any members of the VRS published in the media?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can just tell you about what I know from the time when I was there. I can tell you that General Mladic did not really use the means of communication that we intercepted, not very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anyone ever ask you to -- for permission to broadcast one of your intercepts in order to show what was going on in Zepa and Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I or any of my subordinates were never asked to do anything like that, but whether something like that happened before my time, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us now whether you or any of your subordinates from either the northern or southern location were ever sent for training abroad.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period in question, I state with certainty that none of our men were abroad for any type of training.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever send people abroad for training? Did you propose individuals who should be sent abroad?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period up until 1998, no one was ever sent abroad and there were no proposals to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was training offered for your members, your subordinates, by -- to be conducted by NATO? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not one of my subordinates nor I ever went to a NATO base to undergo any type of training.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I didn't ask whether you went to NATO bases. I just asked whether any of them were sent for training by NATO.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think my answer was clear. No one could leave the unit without my authorisation, which I would have to obtain from my superior command, and that is why I stated with certainty that no one was ever sent for training to any base while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you got some of the notebooks from the logistics section and that some of them you obtained in the village. I want to ask you whether that relates to both the southern and the northern location notebooks?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. All the notebooks would arrive at the unit command where they were then logged and sent to the locations. We didn't check whether they had come from logistics or whatever else. They would all be just registered together and then forwarded on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, you told us a little earlier that they were obtained from logistics or in the village, and I asked you whether this was done -- whether the batches were from the village or -- and whether those bought in the village were sent to both the northern and the southern locations?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those notebooks were purchased in the villages where the command was located, but these were not all the notebooks that we had. And I recall this because I was questioned by my superiors about this and I stated clearly that such notebooks and these notebooks were also purchased from elsewhere. And I've already explained that at that time there were -- there was a batch or a shipment of such notebooks, they appeared in the market, and you could see them everywhere. Whether they came from the humanitarian aid convoys or batches or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, could the Italian manufacturer actually distribute these notebooks in Bosnia and Herzegovina and sell them there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know whether the producer -- manufacturer could or couldn't do that, but they were in the market. You could find them in the market at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just answer this question, please: Did any of your members from either the northern or southern location travel to Italy and did you travel to Italy?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would love to travel to Italy and I hope that I get an opportunity soon because one of my nephews lives there, but I never had that opportunity until now and none of my men did. And during the time when I was the commander of that unit, none of my men travelled to Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this notebook 1D131 into evidence and I would like to tender this book into evidence, 1D128 and 1D126.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction: 1D36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is 1D36 on the screen at the moment? Is there a translation? There's no translation. Is there a translation pending?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is a document that was tendered by the Prosecution. 1D136, 136. Now, we've asked for this document to be uploaded into e-court, and now I would like to tender it into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is clear. We have your indication. The Defence list of potential exhibits for this witness, and there you indicated that translation of this document is pending. And this is the reason why I asked you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering only this page on the -- we have on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. President, I'm tendering both the first and the second page if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I understand --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we will obtain a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand the situation that a translation is not necessary because of the content of this document. It will be received. Is there a need to have it under seal, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the second page of the document contains the location of the site, so I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D136 is now Exhibit D47, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the other document you tender, which was it? 1D126. Is that correct? No, 128. It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D48, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber has reviewed this notebook. Of course we are not experts in printing and handwriting, but after first view it seems to be except the following everything was printed and covered by a kind of plastic cover, except the portions the witness has indicated under the headline "Carta Di Identita Dei Popoti," there is a handwriting number 14 and then a certain number, it's not legible for me. And then at the end in this line, the number 100 plus 450 and then two letters, TS maybe. And then we have this big number 84 with an underlining and on the left side a number, a typical number of the OTP. If you want further investigation, you should move for that in writing. This is to clarify the situation. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Only very briefly, Mr. President. I guess I might as well pick up where you are, and that relates to this, I think it's D47 that's just been marked, which is the notebook in question. I don't know if other than the two pages are uploaded in the e-court, but I would like to turn to the third page if we can. We can no longer do that? Oh, only the two pages are in. May I use the original notebook for a moment, then, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Please hand it over to Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is I'd like to show this to the witness and then if we could place it on the ELMO and we can go to the third page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to know if it's possible to place side by side - maybe not - the image from the ELMO against an exhibit in e-court. I will do them sequentially, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, first have you had an occasion to look at the book and can you tell us whether or not, in your opinion, it's an original or if it's not an original book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have it on the ELMO at the moment. Something happened. It disappeared. Now we have it again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. Looking at the book, can you tell us whether or not, in your opinion, it's an original book or if it's not?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This book is absolutely an original dating from 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what I'd like to refer you to in particular is the number that's on the screen now, which reads: "STR POV BR," and then it reads "08/2-01-161" and it appears to say -- to be dated 12.04.95. Do you see that on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And tell us what that number is.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number is a strictly confidential number, 08/2, that is the number assigned by the competent command to each and every unit every year. This is a registry number assigned to a unit, 08/2. That number varied. As for the other numbers, they indicated certain issues, and the last number, 161, is the number under which this was logged in the log-book in the unit where I worked. Below that we see the date when this was logged and this notebook was sent in this form to the locations. Because we had an insufficient number of men at the command, normally each page should be logged under a number and the last page should also bear the signature or the date when that individual, a platoon commander or a unit commander at the location, actually logged that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would the logging of the book take place before the entries that are made in the book?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be logged before any entries were made in the book. There were times when we found notebooks that lay around from earlier and where we would subsequently log those notebooks. But normally all the notebooks that we obtained, they would be logged and then sent to the locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have, please, P285 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can this notebook be removed from the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to have it there just for a moment longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it should be page 4 in e-court is what I'm looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While that's loading, Witness, was the purpose of the registration of the notebooks done for the purpose of -- was the purpose of registering the notebooks so that they could be identified at a later point in time?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time no one knew -- we had no clue why or what those notebooks would be used for. But as I already said, when I arrived there and on orders from my superiors, we wanted to bring some order into the whole thing so we wanted to register these books and bring some order here. And this was simply the period when we tried to bring some real military order there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just blow up the entry in this exhibit number that's marked -- denominated number 84 and what I'd like to do is compare that to the number that's in the book itself. If we could focus in just a little bit just on the number 84 so it's very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the number that's indicated under 84 in this entry which you've indicated previously was a list of documents that you compiled that were transferred to the representatives of The Hague in 1998 reads as follows: "STR POV 08/2-01-161," and it's dated 12.04.95. Does that correspond to the entry that's in the notebook in front of you right now? I mean the physical notebook. So you can pick it up and take a look and see if it matches.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said about the heading of this notebook, and I can see now that it is the identical number that was logged here. But I also mentioned that the 84 -- the number 84 was entered later on in 1998. That was just a sequential number, and in order to make things even clearer, we also indicated the format of the notebook so that you can easily single them out by just looking at them. So we see that this format of this notebook was A5, which means that it's a small-sized notebook. And then further to the right in the columns we should also see the dates when the first entries were made in that notebook and when the last ones were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you have any doubt whether the book that's in front of you now is the book that's recorded in the log that you prepared in 1998?

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I have no doubts whatsoever, and a little earlier I saw - because this is the first time that I have had this notebook in my hands since the war - I saw another signature in this notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will understand that by looking at some of the information I'm kind of taken back into that time. You will see that there is another signatory there. I can tell you his name because I recognise his signature. And when this individual counted the sheets that were filled, he saw that there were 52 sheets and he placed the date there and his signature. That's one of the heads of the department. If you want me to state his name, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You don't need to state his name right now because we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: PW-032 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My question is: What is the relevance of a document produced in 1998 to the events we are discussing here and the intercepts from back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye is re-examining. Please carry on but bear in mind we are really running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. President. Thank you very much. Just for the record, this reflects the last page of the notebook, which is on the ELMO. The ERN number indicated is 0078-9575. I think I will tender the whole book, but I just want the record to be clear as to what the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to ask you a couple of other questions because we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, you don't have time for that. I am very sorry. We are over time already for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, I wasn't aware of that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The courtroom will be used this afternoon by another Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No problem. No problem, Mr. President. Then this will conclude my examination, except I will tender the notebook in full so that it's clear for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding. It is -- it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P304, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This concludes the questioning for you, sir. You will be pleased that you are now free to return to your normal activities, but please be patient for one minute and sit down so that we can raise all together. I would like to mention two things. We should be more aware of the time we have available. We are only sitting three days a week and it was not very satisfactory by both parties because there was an extended use of time. It was indicated four hours by each party, but each party used more time. And in future, both parties - and bearing in mind the situation of today - especially, Mr. Tolimir, you should think about a better use of time. We are not only -- we have not only to guarantee a fair trial, but also an expeditious trial. And we have a big trial and therefore we should use the time in the most practical way we can. Yesterday I asked the Defence if they have any objections to the Prosecution's supplemental motion for leave to amend its 65 ter exhibit list with two additional exhibits. You indicated that you would respond today so that we can make a decision. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that my legal advisor has already informed the Prosecution of our position, and that is that we have no objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to the admission. And I would like to thank the witness and everybody else who assisted us in the courtroom today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have to adjourn and resume next Tuesday at 9.00 in Courtroom II. Thank you very much. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
